title: India’s Brutal Heatwave Is a Warning for NRIs Planning Summer Trips Home
excerpt: With temperatures crossing 48°C in Uttar Pradesh and at least 18 dead from heatstroke, the worst of India’s summer is here. What the diaspora needs to know before booking that flight.
body:
Every summer, millions of NRIs board flights to India for weddings, family reunions, and long-overdue visits home. This year, the subcontinent is greeting them with a heat so ferocious that it has killed people, shuttered schools across half a dozen states, and pushed national power demand to an all-time record.

Banda, a small city in Uttar Pradesh, recorded 48.2°C on Tuesday — making it the hottest place in India and among the hottest anywhere on Earth this week. Delhi is forecast to hit 45°C by Wednesday, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issuing severe heatwave warnings for at least a dozen states stretching from Rajasthan and Punjab through Madhya Pradesh and into Andhra Pradesh. There is no relief expected until at least May 25.

## A Deadly Toll

The human cost is climbing. At least 18 people have died from confirmed heatstroke in Odisha alone, with 36 additional suspected heat-related deaths under investigation. Schools in Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, and West Bengal have been shut or moved to morning-only schedules. India’s power grid, meanwhile, hit a new peak demand of 257.37 GW on Monday as hundreds of millions of air conditioners and coolers strained the national infrastructure.

The IMD defines a heatwave as temperatures at least 4.5°C above normal. Much of north India is currently running 5°C or more above seasonal averages — a departure that transforms the routine discomfort of an Indian summer into genuine danger.

## Why NRIs Are Especially Vulnerable

For diaspora Indians who have spent years in air-conditioned offices in New Jersey, London, or Toronto, the adjustment to 45°C-plus heat can be physiologically brutal. Bodies that have acclimatised to temperate climates lose their heat tolerance within months of leaving India. The risks are compounded for older NRIs visiting family, for children born abroad who have never experienced an Indian summer, and for anyone travelling with chronic conditions such as diabetes or heart disease.

Dehydration, heat exhaustion, and heatstroke can escalate with terrifying speed. The progression from mild headache to confusion and organ failure can happen within hours if warning signs are ignored.

## What You Should Do

**Before you fly:** Check the IMD forecast for your destination (mausam.imd.gov.in). If your trip overlaps with red or orange alerts, consider adjusting dates if possible — the monsoon typically reaches Kerala by late May and spreads north through June, bringing dramatic cooling.

**On the ground:** Stay indoors between 11 AM and 4 PM. Drink water continuously — not just when thirsty. ORS sachets (available at any chemist) are far more effective than plain water for preventing dehydration. Carry a hat, UV-protection sunglasses, and light cotton or linen clothing. Avoid alcohol during the hottest hours.

**For elderly parents:** If you are visiting ageing parents, check that their home has adequate cooling and ventilation. Power cuts remain common outside metro cities during peak load hours. Portable battery-operated fans and a stash of frozen water bottles can be lifesavers.

**Travel insurance:** Ensure your policy explicitly covers heat-related medical emergencies and, critically, emergency medical evacuation. Standard travel policies sometimes exclude climate-related health events.

## The Monsoon Is Coming — But Not Yet

There is a light at the end of the tunnel. The IMD has forecast the southwest monsoon to reach Kerala around May 26, with a margin of error of four days in either direction. Once the monsoon sets in, it typically takes three to four weeks to sweep across the subcontinent, bringing relief to the northern plains by late June or early July.

Until then, India’s summer remains a gauntlet. For the diaspora, the message is simple: go home, hug your family, attend the wedding — but respect the heat. It is not the same summer you remember.
